terms.definition: A fast mathematical approximation of an expensive simulation or experiment, trained on a small set of known data points. Also called a response surface, metamodel, or emulator.
A mathematical surface mapping input variables to output variables. A surrogate model is a type of response surface. The term originates from experimental design in chemical engineering.
The subset of data used to fit a surrogate model. Typically 70–90% of the available data. The model learns input-output relationships from this set.
The held-out subset of data used to evaluate a trained model on unseen inputs. Kept strictly separate from training. Test set metrics measure how the model generalises.
When a model memorises the training data too closely and performs poorly on new inputs. Signs: high training R² but low test R², or large residuals on test points.
When a model is too simple to capture the true input-output relationship. Low R² on both training and test sets.
Predicting outputs for inputs that lie within the range of the training data. Surrogates are generally reliable here.
Predicting outputs for inputs outside the training data range. Accuracy degrades rapidly — the toolkit flags these with a caution warning.
A design parameter or independent variable fed into the model — e.g., Mach number, angle of attack, material thickness. Also called a feature or predictor.
A quantity of interest predicted by the model — e.g., lift coefficient, von Mises stress, fuel burn. Also called a response or target.

A probabilistic surrogate that places a prior distribution over functions. Provides native uncertainty estimates (posterior standard deviation) alongside predictions. Best for smooth responses with ≤ 2,000 training points.

Originated in geostatistics; mathematically equivalent to GPR with specific kernel choices. In this toolkit, Kriging is unified with GPR — selecting the Matérn 1.5 or 2.5 kernel in the GPR model is equivalent to what was previously called Kriging.
An ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample with a random feature subset. Robust, non-parametric, handles non-smooth responses well. Uncertainty estimated via tree variance.
Interpolates by summing radial basis functions centred at each training point. Deterministic — no uncertainty. Very fast to evaluate and always passes exactly through training points.

Represents the output as a polynomial in the inputs using orthogonal basis functions. Analytically tractable — first-order Sobol sensitivity indices (S₁) are free byproducts derived directly from the polynomial coefficients. Best for smooth, well-behaved responses.
Fits a linear combination of inputs to the output. Extremely fast. Only appropriate when the true relationship is approximately linear. Ridge regularisation avoids overfitting.
A weighted combination of two or more individual surrogates. More robust on complex responses than any single model. Weights can be equal, CV-performance-based, or learned via stacking.

In GPR/Kriging, encodes how similar two outputs are for nearby inputs. Common choices: RBF (infinitely smooth), Matérn 5/2 (twice differentiable), Matérn 3/2 (once differentiable), Rational Quadratic (mixture of scales).
A small diagonal term added to the GPR covariance matrix. Improves numerical stability and allows the model to treat observations as noisy rather than exact. Higher alpha = more noise tolerance.
Fraction of output variance explained by the model. 1.0 is perfect; below 0 means the model is worse than predicting the mean. Rule of thumb: ≥ 0.95 excellent, 0.85–0.95 good, 0.70–0.85 acceptable.
Square root of the mean squared prediction error, in the same units as the output. Heavily penalises large individual errors.
Average of the absolute prediction errors, in the same units as the output. More robust to outliers than RMSE.
Scatter plot of true values (x-axis) vs. predicted values (y-axis). A perfect model falls on the 45° diagonal. Deviations from the diagonal reveal bias; scatter reveals variance.

Scatter plot of true values (x-axis) vs. prediction error (y-axis). Ideally centred at zero with no pattern. Curved residuals suggest a missing non-linear trend; funnel shapes suggest heteroscedasticity.

Non-constant variance in prediction errors — the spread of residuals changes with the output value. Visible as a funnel shape in the residual plot (widening at higher values). Common in physical responses where absolute error scales with magnitude. Can be addressed by log-transforming the output before training.
Technique to estimate model accuracy without consuming test data. The training set is split into k folds; the model trains on k-1 folds and evaluates on the held-out fold, rotating through all k.
Cross-validation with k equal-sized folds. k=5 is standard for datasets of 50+ rows. Balances bias and variance in the CV accuracy estimate.
Special case of k-fold where k equals the number of training points. Ideal for very small datasets (< 30 rows) but expensive for GP models.

A model setting chosen before training that controls complexity — e.g., number of trees in RF, kernel type in GPR, regularisation strength in Ridge. Distinguished from parameters learned during training.
Exhaustive search over a predefined grid of hyperparameter combinations using cross-validation. Finds the combination with the highest mean CV R².
The fraction of data reserved as a held-out test set. Common values: 0.15–0.25. Larger split = better generalisation estimate but smaller training set.

A kernel configuration where each input dimension has its own length-scale parameter. Inputs with large fitted length scales contribute little to the covariance — effectively suppressed by the kernel. Allows GPR to automatically downweight irrelevant inputs during training without manual removal. Fitted length scales are shown in the Results panel after training.

The number of independent starting points used when optimising GPR kernel hyperparameters (length scales, noise). Each restart runs a full L-BFGS-B optimisation from a different random initialisation. More restarts reduce the risk of converging to a poor local optimum, at the cost of proportionally longer training time. Editable in the hyperparameter panel (default: 10).
Rescaling input or output values before training. Prevents columns with large magnitudes from dominating distance-based models such as GPR and RBF.
Maps each column so its minimum = 0 and maximum = 1. Preserves distribution shape. Sensitive to outliers that extend the range.
Transforms each column to mean 0 and standard deviation 1. More robust to outliers than min-max.
Q3 − Q1, the spread of the middle 50% of a distribution. The toolkit flags rows outside Q1 − k×IQR or Q3 + k×IQR as outliers (default k = 1.5).
A data point unusually far from the bulk of the distribution, defined by the IQR criterion. Outliers can distort model fits but may represent physically meaningful extreme conditions.

An interactive panel that opens when you click a data point in the scatter matrix. Shows every column's value for that row alongside its Z-score — how many standard deviations the value is from the column mean. Cells highlighted in red indicate |Z| > 3 (extreme outlier); amber indicates |Z| > 2. Useful for understanding why a particular row is an outlier before deciding whether to remove it.

Companion columns containing per-observation measurement uncertainty, identified by a '_std' suffix matching an output column name (e.g., 'Cd_std' for 'Cd'). When present and designated as Error columns in the Assign step, the GPR uses these values as per-point noise variances during training rather than a single global alpha. This is called noise weighting or heteroscedastic training.
Applying log(1 + x) to a skewed column. Compresses the long tail, making the distribution more symmetric and reducing the influence of extreme values.
Asymmetry in a distribution. |skew| > 1 is flagged as a candidate for log-transformation. Positive skew = long right tail; negative = long left tail.
Measures linear association between two variables; ranges from −1 to +1. Pairs with |r| ≥ 0.90 are flagged as potentially redundant inputs.

Measures how well one input can be predicted from all other inputs. VIF = 1/(1−R²). VIF < 5 is acceptable; VIF 5–10 is moderate; VIF ≥ 10 is high — the input is nearly redundant. Catches multicollinearity that pairwise Pearson r misses.

When two or more input variables are highly correlated or one is approximately predictable from the others. Destabilises GPR kernel optimisation and distorts sensitivity analysis. Detected by Pearson r (pairwise) and VIF (all-pairs). Addressed by removing inputs or applying PCA.

Projects correlated inputs into uncorrelated principal components. PC1 captures the direction of maximum variance, PC2 the next (orthogonal to PC1), and so on. Retaining k components removes all multicollinearity. Trade-off: components are linear combinations of original variables, losing physical interpretability.

The fraction of total input variance captured by a principal component. PC1's explained variance ratio is largest; subsequent components are smaller. Cumulative explained variance reaching ≥ 90% is the standard criterion for choosing how many components to retain.
A variance-based global sensitivity measure. S₁ (first-order) is the fraction of output variance due to one input alone. ST (total-order) includes all interactions with other inputs.
The fraction of output variance explained by an input acting independently. S₁ ≤ ST always. Low S₁ with high ST means the input only matters through interactions.
Total contribution of an input to output variance, including all interactions. Primary ranking metric: high ST = important, low ST = negligible.
Varies each input from its minimum to its maximum while holding all others at their median value. Shows the main effect of each input. Faster than Sobol but does not capture interactions.
A horizontal bar chart of sensitivity indices sorted by magnitude. Longest bar = most influential input. The toolkit overlays ST (dark) on S₁ (light) to show interaction effects.
An iterative approach where the algorithm recommends which new simulations to run, prioritising regions of high uncertainty or expected improvement. Reduces total simulation cost.
A design where sample points are spread evenly across the input space. Maximises coverage and avoids redundant simulations. Latin hypercube sampling is the standard method.
Divides each input dimension into n equal intervals and places exactly one sample per interval. Guarantees good marginal coverage in every dimension.
Acquisition function balancing exploitation (near current best) and exploration (high uncertainty). Maximising EI guides active learning toward regions likely to improve the surrogate.

A function used in active learning and Bayesian optimization to score candidate points and decide where to sample next. Balances exploration (sampling uncertain regions) and exploitation (sampling near predicted optima). Common choices in this toolkit: Expected Improvement (EI) and Upper Confidence Bound (UCB).

Acquisition function for active learning: UCB(x) = −μ(x) + κ·σ(x). The κ parameter controls the exploration–exploitation balance — higher κ favours exploration of uncertain regions. Default κ=2.0 corresponds to a 95% upper confidence bound. Simpler and more robust than EI when the surrogate is miscalibrated.

An iterative strategy for finding the minimum or maximum of an expensive black-box function with as few evaluations as possible. Each iteration: train or update a surrogate model (typically GPR), maximise an acquisition function to choose the next evaluation point, evaluate, and repeat. The toolkit's Active Learning panel implements Bayesian optimization in objective mode.
In multi-objective optimization, the set of solutions where no objective can be improved without worsening another. Points on the front represent optimal trade-offs.
Using data from two or more simulation fidelity levels together. A cheap low-fidelity model (many runs) provides global trends; an expensive high-fidelity model (few runs) provides corrections.
Multi-fidelity approach: trains a LF surrogate on all LF data, fits an error model on residuals (HF − LF) at HF points. Final prediction = LF prediction + learned correction.
Multi-fidelity model: HF = ρ × f_LF + δ. ρ is a scaling factor (OLS); δ is a GP correction. Provides native uncertainty estimates combining LF and correction uncertainties.
Ensemble strategy where a meta-model is trained on the out-of-fold predictions of base models to learn optimal combination weights. Often more accurate than simple averaging.
